fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The form was used for cakes, bread baskets, and boxed pastries, and each order had a pickup date, a contact number, and a recipient field. The owner asked me to read the entries aloud while she compared them with the printed slips. We kept the forms on a blue clipboard beside the flour ledger and marked changes in pencil so the counter staff could see what needed checking before they packed anything. The shop was busy, but the back table was clear enough to lay out the slips in date order.

One order was for a small lemon cake with a pale green border and a short message across the top. The customer had asked for the cake to be boxed separately from two loaves of rye bread and a paper bag of almond twists. The person who placed the order had used her own card for payment, but she had named someone else as the person collecting it. She called before opening time and said, “Please write Quentin, not Mina, in the recipient box because Quentin is collecting the order and Mina is only paying.” She repeated that the cake should stay chilled until the named person arrived. I read the instruction back to her, and she said, “Yes, that is right. The name on the card does not tell you who is picking up the food.”

Section One: Pickup Details listed the order number as four hundred and seventeen, the requested time as half past three, and the recipient as Quentin Rowe. The first copy had Quentin entered in the correct box, but a second slip from the counter showed Mina Rowe in the same place. Her surname was spelled the same way on both slips, so the difference was not a spelling question. I set the two papers side by side and checked the order number and the phone number against the inbox message. Both matched. The message also said that the payer could be contacted about a balance, but that collection questions should go to Quentin. The form had separate boxes for payer and recipient, although the labels were printed in small type.

On the first slip, someone had written the cardholder name across the top margin and then copied it into the recipient box. The handwriting was neat, and there was no correction mark to show why the name had moved. The second slip had been printed later that morning and carried the recipient name from the original message. I did not know who had prepared the first copy, so I left the handwriting as it was and added a pencil note beside the field for the owner to review. She checked the message herself and said the form should keep both roles visible rather than treating the person who paid as the person who would arrive. She did not ask me to change the order details or the pickup time.

The cake decorator had already written the requested message on a small card and placed it beside the cake board. The words were for a birthday, but the customer had not given an age or asked for candles. The decorator said, “I have left the top clear around the lettering so the border can be finished after lunch.” She had used the pale green color from the sample sheet and had set the cake box on the lower refrigerator shelf. The rye loaves were on a separate rack, and the almond twists were still cooling near the oven. I checked that the order number on the card matched the number on the form without moving any of the food or changing the packing notes.

We then looked at the other entries due that afternoon because the same recipient box had been confusing on two earlier orders. One was a bread basket sent to an office, and the other was a tray of small fruit tarts for a family lunch. Those customers had each named a collector different from the person who paid. The office order gave the receptionist as the recipient and the payer in a separate field. The tart order named a cousin and included a phone number for the person placing it. The owner said the printed labels should make those distinctions easier to read, but she had not yet decided whether to request a new form. I wrote down the two examples on the back of the daily count sheet so she could raise them at the next staff meeting.

A little before noon, Quentin came into the shop to ask whether the pickup could be made at half past three rather than closer to closing time. He said he had a work appointment afterward and wanted to check the timing before he left the neighborhood. I found order four hundred and seventeen on the clipboard and told him the form showed the requested time. He said that was what he expected and asked whether the rye bread and twists were attached to the same order. I read the three items from the packing note, and he confirmed them. He did not ask to see the payment details, and I did not discuss the cardholder name with him. The owner was speaking with a delivery driver near the front door.

After he left, I added the time of his visit to the margin of the office copy and left the recipient field unchanged. The owner asked that the two slips stay together until the counter team had checked which one they would use for the pickup. She put the inbox message behind them and returned the clipboard to the blue hook beside the flour ledger. The decorator kept the cake on the lower shelf, and the other items remained in their usual places. The afternoon counter list still showed order four hundred and seventeen under the half past three pickup slot. The last thing I recorded was that the new form examples were on the back of the count sheet, ready to be discussed at the next staff meeting."}]
